disputes: Body without organs in The Logic of Sense, as shown on the entry (re-read 2026-11-19 against SEP §3.2 and LOS series 27): Intensities in The Logic of Sense? The Stanford Encyclopedia article (revised by Daniela Voss, 2022) reads the book as calling the newborn's “life of intensities-in-motion” the body without organs, and pictures that life with Daniel Stern's image of infant experience, published in 1985. The Stanford article and the book both place the body without organs in the infant: the book sets it in the infant's schizoid position, Klein's position as Deleuze revises it (pp. 187–188), to which, it supposes, the schizophrenic regresses (p. 189), the schizophrenic whose body without organs is Artaud's glorious body (pp. 88, 90). They part only on “intensities”, which the book's pages on it never use. The book gives intensity to the erogenous zones of the surface (p. 225), and its essay on Klossowski calls breaths “pure intensities” (p. 297), a possible bridge. The article says Deleuze draws on “a tradition of developmental psychology” and gives Stern's image as its expression; the intensity wording in that paragraph is Stern's, published sixteen years after the book. Not settled.

Sense-event, “sterile division” or “decoupling”: Sterile division or decoupling? Lester and Stivale translate Deleuze's dédoublement as “sterile division” (p. 31). James Williams translates it “decoupling”, since French has its own word, division, and Deleuze avoids it in this passage: on his reading the paradox cuts a single dry proposition loose from the regress, and its sense drifts off sterile (Williams, p. 55). He also reads the two paradoxes as relaunching each other, so that the alternative between them keeps sense in movement (Williams, p. 55).

Aion-chronos, the present (Badiou and Williams): The present: as James Williams reports it, Alain Badiou, in Logiques des mondes (2006; translated as Logics of Worlds), centres time and ethics on the present, where a subject incorporates into the present of a truth. James Williams calls this a moral “presentism” and argues that Deleuze's two presents answer it: the present of Chronos, where the event strikes the body, and the present of the actor, which counter-actualizes it (p. 168), with eternal ideas working on every present because they are neutral and impassive (Williams, pp. 172–174). Badiou's book has not been read for this entry; his position is given as Williams reports it.

Counter-actualization, guidance for action (open question): Can counter-actualization guide action? James Williams asks whether its principles are too abstract for specific wrongs and too individualistic for an ethics that begins from living with others (Williams, p. 153), and whether replaying events suits an age that can cure and prevent what it once had to bear (Williams, p. 158). He takes up the first question again through the series on the Aion and on univocity (Williams, pp. 169–174); the entry leaves the questions open.

Aion-chronos, one present for the whole (open question, 2026-11-21): One present for the whole? Deleuze gives Chronos a divine present of the whole cosmos (pp. 162–163) and a cosmic present for the Stoic unity of bodily causes (p. 131), and in the twelfth series writes that the universe taken as “the system of all systems, or the abnormal set” admits no fixed present (p. 77). The book may be setting the Stoic cosmos, a unity of causes, apart from the universe as an abnormal set; it does not say so, and no scholar's reading of the point has been read for this entry. Left open.

new_d.text: Deleuze's account, in The Logic of Sense (1969), of sense as a fourth dimension of the proposition: an incorporeal event that subsists in propositions and is attributed to things, at the boundary between the two.

new_text.text: Deleuze presents The Logic of Sense as a series of paradoxes that form the theory of sense, with a privileged place for Lewis Carroll, who first staged those paradoxes, and for the Stoics, who began a new image of what a philosopher is (p. xiii), and calls it an attempt at “a logical and psychological novel” (p. xiv).
Pages of The Logic of Sense are from the translation by Mark Lester with Charles Stivale, edited by Constantin V. Boundas (1990).
He starts from the Stoic division of things into two kinds (pp. 4–5).

On one side are bodies, with their qualities, actions and passions and the states of affairs they make up, which are causes for one another; on the other are the incorporeal effects of these causes, “logical or dialectical attributes” of which one can only say that they “subsist or inhere” (p. 5).
When a scalpel cuts flesh, Émile Bréhier writes in a passage Deleuze quotes, it produces in the flesh a new attribute, being cut, which leaves its properties as they were (p. 5).
Deleuze sets green, a quality of the mixture that tree and air make, beside “to green”, an attribute said of the tree (pp. 6, 21).

Three relations within the proposition are commonly recognized, he writes (pp. 12–15): denotation, its relation to a state of affairs, judged true or false; manifestation, its relation to the person who speaks, with that person's desires and beliefs; and signification, its relation to general concepts and to the propositions that imply it or that it implies.
Each in turn grounds or presupposes another, so that they form what he calls the circle of the proposition (pp. 16–17).
Sense is a fourth dimension (p. 19): what the proposition expresses, an “incorporeal, complex, and irreducible entity, at the surface of things” (p. 19).

Deleuze credits its discovery to the Stoics, and finds it again in the fourteenth century in Gregory of Rimini and Nicholas of Autrecourt and at the end of the nineteenth in Meinong (p. 19); Husserl's name for it is expression (p. 20).

In the eighteenth series he adds that credit for the new frontier between things and propositions should perhaps go to Antisthenes (p. 132), among the Cynics and Stoics in whom he finds a third image of the philosopher, turned toward the surface (pp. 129–133).
new_text.excerpt: “perhaps to Antisthenes that credit must be given” (p. 132)

new_text.text: Sense has no existence outside the proposition that expresses it, yet it belongs as an attribute to the thing or state of affairs, while a proposition's own attribute is its predicate (p. 21).

It is “exactly the boundary between propositions and things” (p. 22), and Deleuze identifies it with the event: “the event is sense itself” (p. 22), so long as the event is kept apart from the state of affairs that realizes it (p. 22).
The fifth series sets out the paradoxes of sense (pp. 28–35).

The sense of what I say can be stated only in another proposition, whose sense needs a further one, a regress Deleuze calls Frege's paradox and also Carroll's (pp. 28–29); sense suspends affirmation and negation, so that “God is” and “God is not” have the same sense (pp. 31–33); and propositions about impossible objects such as square circles have a sense and no signification, so the absurd and nonsense must be kept apart (p. 35).

The second, the paradox of sterile division, arises when the sense of a proposition is extracted as a neutralized double of it (p. 31), and sets a task for later: to “combine the sterility of sense” with “its power of genesis” with respect to the proposition's dimensions (p. 32).

Sense, he argues, is produced by nonsense: a paradoxical element, always displaced and absent from its own place, which appears in one series as an empty square (p. 51), circulates through both series and produces sense in each as an effect (pp. 70–71).

He credits the authors called structuralists with this view of sense as a surface effect and a position effect (p. 71), and welcomes the news “that sense is never a principle or an origin” and is produced (p. 72).
Events bear on problems and define their conditions: “The mode of the event is the problematic” (p. 54).
That nonsense belongs to the surface.
new_text.excerpt: editorial lead-in, resting on the sentences that follow

new_text.text: Because nonsense has “an internal and original relation to sense”, the paradoxical element running through the two series bestows sense on the terms of each (p. 81), and this surface organization, Deleuze writes, has “an extreme and persistent fragility” (p. 81).
new_text.excerpt: “this paradoxical element bestows sense upon the terms of each series” (p. 81)

new_text.text: The thirteenth series describes a second nonsense, which he finds in Antonin Artaud's writing from Rodez and in Louis Wolfson's book on his schizophrenia (pp. 83–90), and he warns against grouping child, poet and madman together (pp. 82–83).
new_text.excerpt: Artaud's letter from Rodez (p. 84); Wolfson (pp. 84–88); “grotesque trinity of child, poet, and madman” (p. 83) (reworded after review, 2026-11-21)

new_text.text: Once the surface splits open, “Nonsense no longer gives sense, for it has consumed everything” (p. 82).
new_text.excerpt: quotation verbatim, p. 82; “the surface has split open” (p. 86)

new_text.text: Words may keep a power of denotation, experienced as empty, and lose their sense, their power to express an incorporeal event (p. 87); the two series disappear, and nonsense “absorbs and engulfs all sense” on both sides (p. 91).
new_text.excerpt: “maintains perhaps a certain power of denotation” (p. 87); “the two series have disappeared” (p. 91) (reworded after review, 2026-11-21)

new_text.text: Deleuze calls this nonsense of the depths sub-sense, a-sense or Untersinn, and keeps it apart from surface nonsense (p. 90): the two surface figures of nonsense, which distribute sense, share nothing with the two plunges into nonsense that engulf it (p. 91).
new_text.excerpt: “Sub-sense, a-sense, Untersinn” (p. 90); “two dives into nonsense” (p. 91)

new_text.text: The nineteenth series returns to the surface.
new_text.excerpt: “we must be led back to the surface” (p. 136)

new_text.text: Pure sense is produced there in relation to a third element, “the nonsense of the surface” (p. 136), and humour, which Deleuze calls “the co-extensiveness of sense with nonsense” and “the art of the static genesis” (p. 141), is the art of that relation.
new_text.excerpt: quotations verbatim, pp. 136, 141 (reworded after review, 2026-11-21)

new_text.text: The fourteenth series takes up that task (pp. 94–99).
Sense results from bodies and their mixtures, and so is always in danger of being “snapped up by its cause” (p. 94).
Following the Stoics, Deleuze gives the event a “double causality” (p. 94): bodies are its cause, and other events its quasi-cause.
The quasi-cause is the paradoxical element of nonsense, which secures “the full autonomy of the effect” (p. 95).

Taken as the effect of bodies, sense is impassible and sterile; taken together with the quasi-cause, it shares in that cause's force and becomes productive, engendering the dimensions of the proposition and what fulfils them: states of affairs, states of the subject, concepts and classes (pp. 95–96).
Deleuze calls “the passage from sterility to genesis” the problem the logic of sense always returns to (p. 97).

Husserl, on his account, found sense impassible again in the noema, and then made its genesis depend on common sense, good sense and the form of a person (pp. 96–98); a genesis of sense needs an impersonal transcendental field, the condition Deleuze takes from Sartre's article of 1937 (pp. 98–99), determined by singularities (p. 99).
The static genesis (series 15–17) shows how sense produces what the circle of the proposition took as given: individuals, persons and concepts, and the proposition's dimensions.
Singularities, impersonal and pre-individual, are distributed over a surface, and Deleuze calls them “the true transcendental events” (pp. 102–103).

In the ontological genesis a world forms where the series around singularities converge, and individuals are constituted in it, each enveloping a finite number of its singularities (pp. 109–110); Leibniz's compossibility is the rule of this convergence, and where series diverge an incompossible world begins (p. 111).
On a second level persons appear: a “thing = x common to several worlds”, such as a “vague Adam” (p. 114), defined by synthetic predicates, from which classes and properties derive (p. 115).
The first stage, he writes, is “the work of sense”, the second “the work of nonsense” (p. 116).

In the logical genesis, denotation relates the proposition to individuals, manifestation to persons, and signification to the classes and properties that depend on persons, though Deleuze denies any simple parallel between the two geneses (pp. 118–119); sense is “doubly generative” (p. 120), engendering the proposition and the things its dimensions bear on.
Sense is then expressed as a problem, which propositions answer (pp. 120–121).

The idea of a static genesis, he writes, resolves the contradiction between sterility and genesis (p. 124): bodies produce sense from their depth by forming surfaces, and sense, once at the surface, shares in the quasi-cause and in turn produces individuation and signification (pp. 124–126).
In the twenty-seventh series Deleuze sets beside it a dynamic genesis, which leads “from states of affairs to events, from mixtures to pure lines” (p. 186).
new_text.excerpt: quotation verbatim, p. 186

new_text.text: James Williams, in his guide to the book (2008), calls the quasi-cause one of Deleuze's rare “heavy and clumsy concepts”, resting on stretched analogies with the physics of surfaces, and then defends it: on his reading the quasi-cause changes the relation of actual things to sense and leaves their measurable properties alone (Williams, p. 130).

He glosses “static” through the French physique statique, “the physics of things in equilibrium”, and reads genesis as the emergence of what is singular, and so open to change, in things already identified (Williams, pp. 124–125); the static genesis works, he writes, by limitation (Williams, p. 126).

He reads the static and dynamic geneses as running in opposite directions, the static leading from virtual to actual and the dynamic from actual to virtual, and calls the dynamic process primary; pure events, he insists, stay primary all the same, through the role they play in producing actual things (Williams, pp. 194–196).
new_text.excerpt: “pure events are primary” (Williams, p. 195); “goes from the actual to the virtual” (p. 195) (reworded after review, 2026-11-21)

new_text.text: He warns against taking sense for meaning: meaning changes with each proposition, and sense stays neutral across them (Williams, p. 56).

He defines sense as variations in the intensity of relations between infinitives such as to spill and to offend (Williams, p. 33); an event leaves each infinitive as it was and changes its relations to the others (Williams, p. 35).
new_text.excerpt: “variations in the intensity of relations of infinitives” (Williams, p. 33); restated p. 50

new_text.text: He writes that “Deleuze separates events and sense” to keep sense independent (Williams, p. 35), where the book says “the event is sense itself” (p. 22).
new_text.excerpt: quotations verbatim (Williams p. 35; LOS p. 22)

new_text.text: Read beside p. 22, the gap looks like one of terms: Williams's event has an actual side (Williams, p. 35), and what he calls pure events he also calls infinitives (Williams, pp. 195–196), while Deleuze's identity holds for the event kept apart from the state of affairs (p. 22).
new_text.excerpt: “the actual side of the event” (Williams, p. 35); “pure events or pure infinitives” (p. 195); the reconciliation is the writer's, marked as such (“looks like”)

new_text.text: Neutrality, on Williams's reading, holds for the infinitive and leaves room for change in what he calls significance: “X is a traitor” and “X is not a traitor” express the same sense, to betray, and need not alter its ties to other infinitives alike, and no rule of negation or modality settles how they alter them (Williams, pp. 56–57).
new_text.excerpt: “the same sense (the infinitive ‘to betray’)” (Williams, p. 57)

new_text.text: Even an impossible object such as the round square has a sense, he argues, since a proposition naming it can set off research in mathematics or philosophy (Williams, pp. 57–58).
new_text.excerpt: “trigger enthusiasm for research in philosophy or mathematics” (Williams, p. 58)

new_text.text: Of the regress of sense he stresses that each new proposition alters the sense of the entire series, so that the regress also multiplies sense: “We always have more sense than we think” (Williams, p. 54).
new_text.excerpt: quotation verbatim, Williams p. 54

sense-event.s: The Logic of Sense (1969), trans. Mark Lester with Charles Stivale (1990), Preface and series 1–11 (pp. xiii–73) and 14–17 (pp. 94–126); James Williams, Gilles Deleuze's Logic of Sense: A Critical Introduction and Guide (2008)

new_d.text: The two readings of time in Deleuze's The Logic of Sense (1969): Chronos, in which only the present exists, and Aion, in which only past and future subsist and divide every present without end.

new_text.text: Deleuze takes the pair from the Stoics, for whom, he writes, time must be grasped twice: entirely as the living present of bodies that act and are acted on, and entirely as divisible without end into past and future, “two simultaneous readings of time” (p. 5).
Pages of The Logic of Sense are from the translation by Mark Lester with Charles Stivale, edited by Constantin V. Boundas (1990).

In Chronos only the present exists, and past and future are relative to a present: what is past or future for one present belongs to a vaster one, up to the divine present of the whole cosmos (pp. 162–163).
It is the time of bodies and their mixtures, and the present measures what bodies and causes do (p. 162).
The time of the present is “a limited but infinite time”, infinite because it is cyclical (p. 61).
Beneath the measured present Deleuze places a becoming-mad of the depths that subverts it, which he calls a bad Chronos (pp. 163–164).

The twelfth series, drawing on the physicist Ludwig Boltzmann, limits the oriented present: Chronos goes from past to future only as one present succeeds another within partial systems, and the universe taken as “the system of all systems” admits no fixed present (p. 77).
new_text.excerpt: “no present can be fixed in a Universe” (p. 77)

new_text.text: The eighteenth series keeps a cosmic present for the Stoic unity of bodily causes, a perfect mixture (p. 131).
new_text.excerpt: “everything is exact in the cosmic present” (p. 131)

new_text.text: In the depths of schizophrenia, the thirteenth series says, the present grows “more contracted as it is filled” (p. 87), the movement of schizophrenia Deleuze later assigns to the bad Chronos (p. 164), and the opposition of poles in that bodily present shares nothing with the contradiction spread over Aion's infinite subdivision (pp. 91–92).
new_text.excerpt: quotation verbatim, p. 87; “opposition of poles in the physical present of bodies” (p. 92) (reworded after review, 2026-11-21)

new_text.text: In Aion the past and the future subsist or inhere, and the instant, “without thickness and without extension”, divides each present into past and future in both directions at once (p. 164).
Aion is “a pure straight line at the surface” (p. 62) and the “eternal truth of time” (p. 165).

It is the time of events and effects (p. 62): the event is always at once “something which has just happened and something about to happen” (p. 63), and of dying Deleuze writes that no one ever dies, and one “has always just died or is always going to die” (p. 63).

He lists the contrasts in the twenty-third series (p. 165): Chronos is limited and infinite, circular, and filled entirely by the bodies that are its causes and matter; Aion is unlimited as past and future are, finite as the instant is, a straight line, and haunted by incorporeal effects that never fill it.
Aion traces the frontier between things and propositions, and in this way makes language possible (pp. 166–167).

On its line Deleuze places an eternal return of pure events, set against the circular return of Chronos (p. 176), and borrows from Borges the image of a labyrinth made of a single straight line (pp. 62, 176).
Aion has a present of its own, the present of “the actor, dancer, or mime” (p. 168), and the pure infinitive of the verb, he writes, is the Aion (pp. 184–185).
What the Stoics brought up to the surface, in the eighteenth series, is the event, different in nature from bodies, and “the Aion in its difference in nature from the devouring Chronos” (p. 132).
new_text.excerpt: quotation verbatim, p. 132

new_text.text: James Williams reads Aion and Chronos as two incompatible times that determine each other, and the theory as depending on never folding them into one time: the event has “an actual passing side” in Chronos and “an eternal but differential side” in Aion, which is how events can be “both eternal and passing” (Williams, pp. 122–123).

He reads the present of the actor that closes the twenty-third series (p. 168) as Deleuze's answer, decades in advance, to an ethics centred on the present act, of the kind Alain Badiou sets out in Logiques des mondes (2006) (Williams, pp. 172–174).

Pages of Williams are from his Gilles Deleuze's Logic of Sense: A Critical Introduction and Guide (Edinburgh University Press, 2008); they are pages of the guide and open nothing in your copy of Deleuze.

aion-chronos.s: The Logic of Sense (1969), trans. Mark Lester with Charles Stivale (1990), series 2 (pp. 4–11), 10, “Of the Ideal Game” (pp. 58–65), and 23, “Of the Aion” (pp. 162–168); James Williams, Gilles Deleuze's Logic of Sense: A Critical Introduction and Guide (2008)

new_d.text: In Deleuze's The Logic of Sense (1969), the operation that doubles an event's actualization in bodies and states of affairs, modeled on the actor, and draws out the event's impersonal part and its eternal truth.

new_text.text: Every event, Deleuze writes, has a double structure (pp. 151–152): on one side the moment it is actualized, embodied in a person, an individual or a state of affairs; on the other its past and future taken in themselves, impersonal and pre-individual, whose only present is the mobile instant that represents it, which he calls the counter-actualization (p. 151).
He credits Maurice Blanchot with showing this double structure in death, which is grounded in me and my body and also has “no relation to me at all” (p. 151).
Pages of The Logic of Sense are from the translation by Mark Lester with Charles Stivale, edited by Constantin V. Boundas (1990).
Deleuze ties this double structure to ethics: only the free man, he writes, grasps the event and enacts its counter-actualization, and so escapes ressentiment (p. 152).

Stoic ethics, Deleuze writes, consists in willing the event as such, whatever occurs insofar as it occurs (p. 143); he later narrows the formula, so that the will wills “something in that which occurs”, which he calls the Event (p. 149).

Ethics either makes no sense at all, he writes, or it means “not to be unworthy of what happens to us” (p. 149); to take what happens as unjust and as someone else's fault is ressentiment, and resignation, he suggests, is one more figure of it (p. 149).
His example is Joe Bousquet, who took the wound he bore as a pure event (p. 148); events, Deleuze writes, signal to us: “My wound existed before me, I was born to embody it” (p. 148).
Deleuze grounds this ethics in the physics of the eighteenth series, to which he returns (p. 143).
new_text.excerpt: “We must go back to what we said a little while ago” (p. 143)

new_text.text: In Stoic physics a mixture is “good in the order of the whole” and can be bad, even execrable, in partial encounters (p. 131), and the hero of Stoic thought is Hercules, who always returns to the surface, from the depths or the heights (pp. 131–132).
new_text.excerpt: “good in the order of the whole, but imperfect, bad, or even execrable” (p. 131); “ascends or descends to the surface” (p. 132)

new_text.text: The sage of the nineteenth series finds at the surface pure events taken in their eternal truth, apart from the state of affairs that actualizes them (p. 136).
new_text.excerpt: “Pure events considered from the perspective of their eternal truth” (p. 136)

new_text.text: The model is the actor (pp. 147, 150).
The actor occupies the instant and plays a role that is always still to come and already past, and so keeps from the event “only its contour and its splendor” (p. 150).

Counter-actualization alone, Deleuze warns, belongs to a buffoon; doubling the event's real actualization, as the true actor and dancer do, it gives the truth of the event “the only chance of not being confused with its inevitable actualization” (p. 161).

In the twenty-second series, which opens on F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Crack-Up, he asks whether one can stop at an event's counter-actualization and prevent its full actualization in the body (p. 157), and answers that the event's eternal truth is grasped only when the event is “also inscribed in the flesh” (p. 161).
Psychoanalysis, the science of pure events in his account, is also, he writes, an art of counter-actualizations (p. 212).

James Williams reads counter-actualization as a replay of the event that leaves its outcome as it was and changes its tone and significance, as Joe Bousquet did with his wound in his books (Williams, p. 155).

What stays as it was is the physical event, the wound, which creation cannot negate; the free act that redoubles it changes the wound's past and future, so that a curtailed youth becomes an entry into poetry (Williams, pp. 155–156).
new_text.excerpt: “Creation cannot negate what occurs” (Williams, p. 155); “changes the past and the future” (p. 156)

new_text.text: In an earlier example, the barricades of June 1832, the first barricade matters to the authorities for the way its sense can be expressed again in later uprisings, and Williams calls counter-actualization “a reciprocally determining interaction between sense and the actual side of events”: acts of repair, on his reading, redouble at the level of sense what was done (Williams, pp. 35–37).
new_text.excerpt: quotation verbatim, Williams pp. 36–37 (runs across the page break)

new_text.text: He renders Deleuze's amor fati as a “love of the event”, which selects something to affirm on the event's ideal side and neither denies nor resents what happened in the body (Williams, p. 156).

He extends it to Deleuze's way of reading philosophers: in his book on Hume, Deleuze divines what in an earlier philosophy crosses the ages and replays it, which Williams calls replaying and counter-actualization and counts as Deleuze's moral position (Williams, p. 203).
new_text.excerpt: “what is meant by replaying and counter-actualisation” (Williams, p. 203)

body-without-organs.old: In The Logic of Sense (1969), the Stanford Encyclopedia article notes, Deleuze drew on Artaud to name a life of intensities in motion the body without organs.
body-without-organs.new: Deleuze had already used it in The Logic of Sense (1969), where it is Artaud's “glorious body”, an organism without parts set against the fragmented body in the depths of schizophrenia (pp. 88, 90, 188). The Stanford Encyclopedia article reads that book as naming with it a life of intensities in motion; the book's pages on the body without organs do not speak of intensity. Pages of The Logic of Sense are from the translation by Mark Lester with Charles Stivale, edited by Constantin V. Boundas (1990).
body-without-organs.by: LOS pp. 88, 90, 188; SEP (as checked in glossary-dg.json and glossary-ao.json); editorial (page note)
body-without-organs.note: The entry's one Logic of Sense sentence, which rested on the Stanford article, read against the book: in it the body without organs is Artaud's glorious body, the active pole of the schizophrenic depths set against the fragmented body (pp. 88, 90, 188); none of the pages naming it (pp. 88–93, 129, 188–203, 224, and note 3 to series 27 on p. 351) speaks of intensity, though the book gives intensity to the erogenous zones of the surface (p. 225) and calls breaths “pure intensities” in its Klossowski appendix (p. 297). The Stanford reading is kept, credited, beside the book. The entry stays audited in glossary-ao.json.

body-without-organs.old: The Stanford Encyclopedia article reads that book as calling the newborn's “life of intensities-in-motion” the body without organs, a life it pictures with Daniel Stern's image of infant experience (1985); the book's pages on the body without organs do not speak of intensity.
body-without-organs.new: The Stanford Encyclopedia article reads that book as calling the newborn's “life of intensities-in-motion” the body without organs, a life it pictures with Daniel Stern's image of infant experience (1985). The book also places it in the infant: in its twenty-seventh series Deleuze takes up Melanie Klein's schizoid position of the nursing infant and revises it: what that position sets against bad partial objects is the body without organs (pp. 187–188), and Deleuze supposes that the schizophrenic regresses to that position (p. 189). They differ on intensity, which the book's pages on the body without organs never mention.
body-without-organs.note: The owner pointed out (2026-11-19) that series 27 also places the body without organs in the infant: the nursing infant of Klein's paranoid-schizoid position (p. 187) sets against bad partial objects an organism without parts, a body without organs (p. 188), and Deleuze supposes the schizophrenic regresses to that position (p. 189; the book puts it as an assumption, 'If we assume'). So the Stanford reading and the book agree on the infant and differ on intensity: no page of series 13 (pp. 88–93), p. 129, or series 27–28 up to p. 200 uses 'intens-' (searched in the OCR text 2026-11-19; pp. 201–203 and 224 rest on the 2026-11-17 reading). Entry sentence and dispute narrowed accordingly.

body-without-organs.note: Added 2026-11-21 (batch 3): set against the fragmented body alone, the glorious body could read as a stable cure; pp. 88–89 make the two poles of one ambivalence. Series 13 calls the breath-words' values “exclusively tonic” (p. 88), not intensities, so the intensity dispute stands as it was. The entry stays audited in glossary-ao.json.

summary: Three new entries read in The Logic of Sense (Lester and Stivale's translation), every quotation verbatim and every page checked: sense and event, Aion and Chronos, and counter-actualization. They describe what the book says and credit no one else's reading, since the encyclopedias could not be fetched and Williams's guide was lost; both are listed as unread. Body without organs now says what The Logic of Sense itself says of it, beside the Stanford reading, and the gap between them is shown as an open dispute. Second batch (2026-11-19): sense and event now covers the sterility and genetic power of sense, double causality and the quasi-cause, and the static genesis; all three entries give James Williams's reading with his pages, and three new open disputes are recorded; body without organs quotes the Stanford article and says where it agrees with the book. Third batch (2026-11-21): series 12–13 and 18–19 read in full. Sense and event now tells the nonsense of the surface, which gives sense, from the nonsense of the depths, which engulfs it, and adds humour, Antisthenes and the dynamic genesis; Aion and Chronos adds the twelfth series' universe without a present and the Stoic cosmic present, with an open question between them; counter-actualization adds the eighteenth and nineteenth series; body without organs adds the action-passion ambivalence. Williams's readings added on the infinitive, neutrality, the regress, impossible objects, the dynamic genesis, Bousquet and the barricades, and reading Hume.

batch3.terminology: Williams writes that “Deleuze separates events and sense” to keep sense independent (Williams, p. 35); Deleuze writes “the event is sense itself” (p. 22). The entry offers, as its own reading and marked as such, that the gap looks like one of terms: Williams's event has an actual side (Williams, p. 35; p. 57 calls it both something expressed and a change in a state of affairs), and what he calls pure events he also calls infinitives (Williams, pp. 195–196), while Deleuze's identity holds for the event kept apart from the state of affairs that realizes it (p. 22). Williams himself does not say this; not shown as a dispute.
